sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Chapter 4 covers drill rigs, overburden and open-hole drilling, grout types with mixing and placing, and reinforcement types. Construction is drilling, placing reinforcement and grouting; for Type A and B micropiles: drill to tip, place steel, tremie the initial grout, add grout under pressure (Type B) (Figure 4-1). Equipment and techniques are similar to those for soil nails, ground anchors and grout holes.
sections.body: (p. 4-1) This chapter familiarizes design engineers and construction personnel with the techniques and materials used to construct micropiles: (1) types of drill rigs; (2) techniques for overburden and open-hole drilling; (3) grout types with methods of mixing and placing; and (4) types of reinforcement. Construction is a succession of processes, the most significant being drilling, placing the reinforcement and grouting, and many of the large number of drilling systems for overburden and rock are used. The typical sequence for simple Type A and B micropiles (Figure 4-1) is drilling the shaft to the required tip elevation, placing the steel reinforcement, placing the initial grout by tremie, and placing additional grout under pressure (Type B). The drilling and grouting equipment and techniques are generally similar to those used for soil nails, ground anchors and grout holes.
key_points: Covers drill rigs, overburden and open-hole drilling, grout mixing and placing, reinforcement types
Main processes: drilling, placing the reinforcement, grouting
Type A/B sequence: drill to tip elevation, place steel, tremie initial grout, add pressure grout (Type B) (Figure 4-1)
Equipment and techniques similar to soil nails, ground anchors and grout holes
sections.applicability: Scope of the construction chapter: drill rigs, drilling, grout, reinforcement.

sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: Most contractor-selected drilling methods are acceptable if they form a stable hole of the required size within tolerance without harming the surroundings; do not exclude a method for not fitting a preconceived approach. Vigorous water flushing can enlarge the bond-zone diameter but risks voids, settlement and hydrofracture heave. Drill, reinforce and grout each pile continuously; in overconsolidated clays and clay shales complete the bond zone within one day. Water supply, cleanliness and hazardous spoil may dictate air flush or augers.
sections.body: (pp. 4-1 to 4-3) Most drilling methods selected by the specialty contractor are likely to be acceptable provided they form a stable hole of the required dimensions, within the stated tolerances and without detriment to the surroundings. A method should not be excluded because it does not suit a predetermined concept of how the project should be executed, and the drilling contractor should know the ground conditions and the effects of the chosen method; drilling on a congested urban site near older buildings or deteriorating foundations has very different constraints from new foundations on an open site. Drilling may disturb the surrounding ground for a certain time and distance; the method should avoid unacceptable disturbance while installing a micropile that supports the required capacities most cost-effectively. Vigorous water flushing can increase drilling rates and remove the fines of mixed soils, enlarging the effective bond-zone diameter and aiding grout penetration and capacity; higher flush flow rates and pressures should be approached with caution because of the risks of voids and surface settlement and of hydrofracturing the ground, which could cause heave. Drilling, reinforcement installation and grouting of a micropile should be a series of continuous processes executed as expeditiously as possible; longer delays can harm the surrounding soil, and materials such as overconsolidated clays and clay shales can deteriorate, relax or soften on exposure and lose bond, so in these cases the bond zone should be completed within one day so that no hole stays open overnight. Water flush may need supply, handling and disposal of large quantities of water, with ponds or tanks for settlement and recirculation where water is scarce; cleanliness requirements or lack of space may dictate air flush or augers, and hazardous materials needing controlled disposal of cuttings may also require augers.
key_points: Any method acceptable if it forms a stable hole of required size within tolerance without harming the surroundings
Do not exclude a method because it does not fit a predetermined concept of the work
Vigorous water flush can enlarge bond-zone diameter, but high flow and pressure risk voids, settlement and hydrofracture heave
Drill, place reinforcement and grout each micropile continuously and expeditiously
Overconsolidated clays and clay shales: complete the bond zone within one day (no hole open overnight)
Scarce water, cleanliness, limited space or hazardous spoil may dictate air flush or augers

sections.title: Drill Rigs
sections.summary: Micropile rigs are hydraulic rotary (electric or diesel) units, usually track mounted; large rigs take long rod and casing sections, small ones work in low overhead (Figures 4-2, 4-3). Frame-mounted drills run off a remote power unit by long hoses (Figure 4-4). With a short mast and short jointed sections, micropiles can be installed with less than 3 m (10 ft) of overhead; a vertical micropile centerline can be about 375 mm (15 in.) from a wall face, more for micropiles larger than about 175 mm (7 in.).
sections.body: (pp. 4-3 to 4-5) Drill rigs typically used for micropiles are hydraulic rotary (electric or diesel) power units. They can be track mounted for maneuverability on difficult and sloped terrain; the size varies greatly (Figures 4-2 and 4-3), larger drills using long sections of rod and casing where there are no overhead restrictions and smaller drills working in lower overhead and harder-to-reach locations. The mast can be mounted on a frame for limited-access, low-overhead areas such as building basements. A frame-mounted drill (Figure 4-4) can be connected by long hoses to a separate hydraulic power unit placed outside the work area, reducing space requirements, noise and exhaust problems; the frame can be moved and supported by fork lift, or moved by hand with winches and supported by bolting to a concrete floor and/or bridge footing or bracing from a ceiling or bridge soffit. The rotary head turning the drill string (casing, augers or rods) can be extremely powerful even on the smallest rigs. Shortening the mast and using short jointed sections of drill string and reinforcement allows installation with less than 3 m (10 ft) of overhead clearance. For a vertical micropile the centerline can be located within approximately 375 mm (15 in.) of the face of an adjacent wall; this distance may need to increase for micropiles larger than approximately 175 mm (7 in.) in diameter.
key_points: Hydraulic rotary (electric or diesel) units, usually track mounted
Large rigs use long rod and casing sections; small rigs work in low overhead (Figures 4-2, 4-3)
Frame-mounted drills run off a remote power unit by long hoses; supported by fork lift, bolting or bracing (Figure 4-4)
Short mast and short jointed sections allow installation with less than 3 m (10 ft) overhead
Vertical micropile centerline can be within about 375 mm (15 in.) of a wall face; more for diameters above about 175 mm (7 in.)

sections.title: Drilling Techniques
sections.summary: Choose the method for minimal disturbance and efficient, reliable penetration. Weak overburden needs overburden techniques; unless the bearing stratum is self-supporting (rock, cohesive soil) the hole may need temporary casing (Figure 4-5) or drilling fluid full length; otherwise open-hole drilling. Existing structures are cored or drilled rotary percussive (Figures 4-6 to 4-8). Water is the commonest flush, then air, slurries, foam; air can fracture and heave ground; bentonite slurry impairs bond; polymer muds work in all ground.
sections.body: (pp. 4-6 to 4-9) The drilling method is selected to cause minimal disturbance or upheaval to the ground and structure while being the most efficient, economic and reliable means of penetration. Micropiles must often be drilled through overlying weak material to a more competent bearing stratum, so overburden drilling techniques are typically needed to penetrate and support weak and unconsolidated soils and fills; unless the bearing stratum is self-supporting, such as rock or a cohesive soil, the hole may need temporary support for its full length, e.g., temporary casing (Figure 4-5) or suitable drilling fluid. If self-supporting material is present for the full depth, the hole can possibly be formed by open-hole techniques without drill casing or hollow-stem auger. Alternative methods are needed to penetrate an existing structure (Figure 4-6): concrete coring can give an oversized hole in slabs and footings for the drill casing; rotary percussive rock drilling can penetrate lightly reinforced footings; rotary percussive (Figure 4-7) or rotary duplex (Figure 4-8) techniques may first penetrate an obstruction layer such as concrete rubble, with single-tube advancement completing the shaft in the soil below. Water is the most common flushing medium, followed by air, drill slurries and foam. Air flush should be used with caution to avoid injecting air into the ground and causing fracturing and heaving. Bentonite slurries impair grout-to-ground bond by creating a skin of clay at the interface, although this is not an uncommon choice in Italian and French practice with Type D piles. Polymer drilling muds have been used successfully in all types of ground, reduce concern for bond impairment and are easier to clean up and dispose of than bentonite.
key_points: Select for minimal disturbance and the most efficient, economic, reliable penetration
Weak overburden needs overburden techniques; temporary casing (Figure 4-5) or drilling fluid unless the bearing stratum is self-supporting
Open-hole techniques possible where self-supporting material extends the full depth
Existing structures: concrete coring, rotary percussive or rotary duplex through obstructions (Figures 4-6 to 4-8)
Flush: water most common, then air, slurries, foam; air can fracture and heave the ground
Bentonite slurry impairs grout-to-ground bond (still used in Italian and French Type D practice); polymer muds used successfully in all ground

sections.title: Overburden Drilling Techniques
sections.summary: Seven generic overburden methods are common for piles under 300 mm (12 in.) to depths under 60 m (200 ft) (Table 4-1; Figure 4-9): single-tube advancement (drive drilling, not used for micropiles; external flush wash boring), rotary duplex, rotary percussive concentric duplex, rotary percussive eccentric duplex (ODEX), double head duplex, hollow-stem auger (post grouting essential, Type D) and sonic (50 to 150 Hz). Wash boring under sensitive structures must not cause cavitation; air flush risks ground disturbance.
sections.body: (pp. 4-9 to 4-13) There are many proprietary overburden drilling systems, and specialty contractors develop their own variations, but seven generic methods are common for piles less than 300 mm (12 in.) in diameter to depths less than 60 m (200 ft); they are summarized in Table 4-1 and Figure 4-9. Single-tube advancement, external flush (wash boring): the casing toe has an open crown or bit and is rotated into the ground with continuous water flush through the casing, the debris usually escaping around the outside of the casing but possibly lost into very loose, permeable strata; care is needed below sensitive structures so that uncontrolled washing does not cause cavitation; air flush is not normally used because of the danger of over-pressurizing the ground; polymer flush additives can be very advantageous in certain ground (Bruce, 1992) and do not appear to harm bond as bentonite may. Rotary duplex: the drill rod and bit inside the casing are on the same rotary head, rotated and advanced together; flush (usually water or polymer) goes down the rod and returns up the rod-casing annulus; air flush must be used with caution because annulus blockages can build high air pressure at the bit. Rotary percussive duplex (concentric): rods and casing are percussed, rotated and advanced together by a top-drive rotary percussive head of substantial energy. Rotary percussive duplex (eccentric or lost crown), originally sold as ODEX: an eccentric underreaming bit undercuts the casing, which is pushed into the oversized hole with much less energy, needs no expensive cutting shoe and wears less; larger sizes, over 127 mm (5 in.), often use a down-the-hole hammer on a drive shoe so the casing is pulled in. Double head duplex: rods and casing are turned by separate heads in opposite directions, giving high torque at low speed, high penetration rates, less annulus blockage and exceptional hole straightness even in the most difficult ground. Hollow-stem auger: continuous flight auger with a capped hollow core, installed by purely rotary heads; grout is placed through the stem as the auger is withdrawn; used in cohesive materials, very soft rocks and commonly sands, but in sands with minimal cohesion there is a danger of loosening or cavitating the soil, especially in inclined holes, so post grouting is essential (Type D); heavy obstructions are hard to penetrate economically, and uncontrolled penetration or excessive hole cleaning risks loosening. Sonic (rotosonic, rotasonic, sonicore, vibratory or resonant sonic): a dual-cased system vibrating the whole drill string at 50 to 150 hertz to core overburden and most bedrock and advance casing.
key_points: Seven generic overburden methods for piles under 300 mm (12 in.) to depths under 60 m (200 ft) (Table 4-1, Figure 4-9)
Wash boring (single-tube, external flush): avoid uncontrolled washing under sensitive structures; air flush not normally used
Rotary duplex: rod and casing on one head, flush up the annulus; air flush with caution (blockage builds pressure at the bit)
Rotary percussive concentric duplex: needs a powerful top rotary percussive head
Eccentric duplex (ODEX): eccentric bit underreams; casing over 127 mm often pulled by a down-the-hole hammer
Double head duplex: counter-rotating rods and casing; fast, straight drilling in very difficult ground
Hollow-stem auger: risk of loosening sands, especially inclined holes; post grouting essential (Type D)
Sonic: whole string vibrated at 50 to 150 Hz; little or no flush; full-length sample recovered
figures: Figure 4-9: Overburden Drilling Methods (modified after Bruce, 1989) (p. 4-9)
tables: Table 4-1: Overburden Drilling Methods (after Bruce, 1989): 1a drive drilling, casing with lost point percussed without flush, 50-100 mm to 30 m (2-4 in. to 100 ft), obstructions or very dense soil problematic (not described in the text, no application in micropile construction); 1b external flush, casing with shoe rotated with strong water flush, 100-250 mm to 60 m (4-10 in. to 200 ft), needs high torque head and powerful flush pump; 2 rotary duplex, 100-220 mm to 70 m (4-8.75 in. to 230 ft), very sensitive soil/site conditions, positive flush return, high torques; 3 rotary percussive concentric duplex, 89-175 mm to 40 m (3.5-7 in. to 130 ft), obstructed/rocky conditions; 4 rotary percussive eccentric duplex, 89-200 mm to 60 m (3.5-8 in. to 200 ft), expensive, difficult overburden; 5 double head duplex, 100-150 mm to 60 m (4-6 in. to 200 ft), fast straight drilling in very difficult ground; 6 hollow-stem auger, 100-400 mm to 30 m (4-16 in. to 100 ft), obstructions problematic, prevents higher grout pressures; 7 sonic, 100 to 300 mm to 100 m (4-12 in. to 330 ft), no or minimal flush, full-length sample (p. 4-10)

sections.title: Open Hole Drilling Techniques
sections.summary: In stable, free-standing ground the casing can stop and the hole continue open (a trade-off between changeover time and overburden drilling cost). Rotary percussive: for strong rock, down-the-hole hammers most economical at micropile diameters (air, mist or foam flush); top-drive hammers are noisy and may damage structures by vibration. Solid core continuous flight auger: stiff to hard clays without boulders and some weak rocks; rapid, quiet, no flush, but possible decompression or smear. Underreaming is rare.
sections.body: (p. 4-13) When a micropile can be formed in stable, free-standing conditions, casing advancement may be suspended and the hole continued by open-hole techniques, balancing the time lost changing to a less expensive open-hole system against continuing the more expensive overburden system. Rotary percussive drilling: particularly for rocks of high compressive strength, using top-drive or down-the-hole hammers; for small micropile diameters down-the-hole techniques are the most economical and common, with air, air/water mist or foam flush; top-drive systems have limited diameter and depth capacities, are relatively noisy and may damage the structure or foundation by excessive vibration. Solid core continuous flight auger: in stiff to hard clays without boulders and some weak rocks; rapid, quiet, needs no flushing medium, but there may be lateral decompression or wall remolding/interface smear that can harm grout-to-ground bond; useful where careful collection and disposal of spoil is important. Underreaming: tools enlarge or underream open holes in cohesive soils or soft sediments, especially for tension micropiles, cutting single or multiple bells; it is time-consuming, its effectiveness is rarely verifiable, cleaning is difficult (water may soften the ground), so it is rare in typical micropile practice.
key_points: In stable, free-standing ground casing can stop and the hole continue open (cost trade-off)
Rotary percussive for strong rock: down-the-hole hammers most economical for micropile diameters; top-drive noisy, may damage structures by vibration
Solid core continuous flight auger: stiff to hard clays without boulders, weak rocks; no flush; risk of decompression or smear
Underreaming: time-consuming, hard to verify and clean; rare in typical micropile practice
sections.applicability: Open-hole methods once the hole is stable: rotary percussive, solid-stem auger, underreaming.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Grouts must be strong, stable (low bleed) and pumpable: w/c 0.40 to 0.50 by weight (Figure 4-10), potable water, Type I/II cement (ASTM C150/AASHTO M85), usually neat cement; bentonite only with extreme caution. Neat grouts reach 28 to 35 MPa (4,000 to 5,000 psi). Grout to refusal; a take over twice the neat hole volume warrants attention. If Type B pressure cannot be held, pump to the pile top; keep pressure at 0.70 MPa (100 psi) or less; proof tests (Chapter 7) on suspect piles.
sections.body: (pp. 4-14 to 4-16) Grouting operations have a major impact on micropile capacity (Chapter 2). Grouts are designed for high strength and stability (bleed) but must be pumpable, implying typical water/cement ratios of 0.40 to 0.50 by weight (Figure 4-10, where bleed capacity is the free water at final set: at w/c 1.0, 100 liters of grout develop 20 liters of free water). Grouts use potable water to reduce the danger of reinforcement corrosion. Type I/II cement (ASTM C150/AASHTO M85) is most common, bagged or bulk. Neat cement-water grouts are most common, though sand is a common additive in some countries (e.g., Italy, Britain); bentonite, which reduces strength, is used in primary mixes only with extreme caution, and additives only where improved pumpability is needed (long distances, hot conditions; e.g., high-range water reducers). Properly produced neat cement grouts attain design compressive strengths of 28 to 35 MPa (4,000 to 5,000 psi). Admixtures and additives must be chemically compatible, best by using one chemical supplier. The grout transfers load between reinforcement and ground, may form part of the load-bearing section, protects the steel from corrosion, and may act beyond the hole by permeation, densification and/or fissuring, so it needs adequate fluidity, strength, stability and durability; raising water content for fluidity harms the other three, and w/c is the most important factor, limited to 0.40 to 0.50 (additives may be needed for pumpability below 0.40). There must be no significant grout loss from any part relied on for load or corrosion protection, achieved by grouting to refusal; grout loss may need a filler such as sand, or pre-grouting, redrilling and regrouting; loss is judged from the grout level after stiffening, and a take over twice the neat hole volume indicates voided or very permeable conditions warranting special attention. For Type B micropiles the soil seal around the casing may not hold the desired pressure, sometimes after partial pressure grouting of the bond length; the grout should then be pumped to the top of pile and grouting stopped; keeping pressures at 0.70 MPa (100 psi) or less helps. If test micropiles were grouted full length at the desired pressure, partially pressure-grouted production piles may be questioned; testing to typically 150 to 200 percent of design load or more helps show excess capacity, and production proof tests (Chapter 7) may be run on suspect piles. A grout quality control plan, at minimum cube or cylinder compression and grout density (w/c) testing, is in Chapter 8. Guides: Littlejohn (1982), Gourlay and Carson (1982), Houlsby (1990); for ground anchors, Littlejohn and Bruce (1977).
key_points: Grout must be strong, stable (low bleed) and pumpable: w/c 0.40 to 0.50 by weight (Figure 4-10)
Potable water; Type I/II cement (ASTM C150/AASHTO M85); neat cement grout most common; bentonite only with extreme caution
Properly produced neat cement grouts reach design strengths of 28 to 35 MPa (4,000 to 5,000 psi)
Use chemically compatible admixtures, ideally from one supplier
Grout transfers load, may carry load, protects steel, may permeate or densify the ground
Grout to refusal; a take over twice the neat hole volume indicates voided or very permeable ground
Type B: if pressure cannot be held, pump to pile top and stop; keep pressures at 0.70 MPa (100 psi) or less
Testing to 150-200 % of design load helps judge partially pressure-grouted piles; proof tests (Chapter 7) on suspect piles
Grout QC plan (Chapter 8): at least cube or cylinder strength and density (w/c) tests

sections.title: Grout Equipment
sections.summary: Any plant suited to mixing and pumping fluid cement grout may be used; the best grouts come from high-speed, high-shear colloidal mixers (Figure 4-11) rather than paddle mixers (Figure 4-12). Lower-pressure injection, up to 2 MPa (290 psi) and 200 liters/min (52 gal/min), usually uses constant-pressure rotary-screw pumps (e.g., Moyno); higher-pressure Type C or D grouting usually needs a piston or ram pump delivering up to 8 MPa (1,160 psi) at up to 50 liters/min (13 gal/min).
sections.body: (pp. 4-16 to 4-18) In general, any plant suitable for mixing and pumping fluid cementitious grouts may be used. The best quality grouts, in both fluid and set properties, are produced by high-speed, high-shear colloidal mixers (Figure 4-11) rather than low-speed, low-energy paddle mixers (Figure 4-12); high-speed mixers are faster and produce a homogeneous mix (Section 4.3.3). Mixers can be driven by air, diesel or electricity and come in many capacities and sizes. For placement, lower pressure injection (up to 2 MPa (290 psi) and up to 200 liters/min (52 gal/min)) usually uses constant-pressure rotary-screw pumps (e.g., Moyno pumps), while higher pressure grouting, such as for Type C or D micropiles, usually needs a fluctuating-pressure piston or ram pump delivering up to 8 MPa (1,160 psi) at up to 50 liters/min (13 gal/min).
key_points: Any plant suited to mixing and pumping fluid cement grout may be used
High-speed, high-shear colloidal mixers give the best grout (Figure 4-11); paddle mixers less so (Figure 4-12)
Lower pressure, up to 2 MPa (290 psi) and 200 L/min (52 gal/min): rotary-screw pumps (e.g., Moyno)
Type C or D: piston or ram pumps, up to 8 MPa (1,160 psi) at up to 50 L/min (13 gal/min)
figures: Figure 4-11: Various Types of High Speed, High Shear 'Colloidal' Mixers (p. 4-17)
Figure 4-12: Various Types of Paddle Mixers (p. 4-18)

sections.title: Grout Mixing
sections.summary: Add water first, then cement, then aggregate or filler; mix for at least two minutes, then keep in slow agitation in a holding tank. Ready-mix only for exceptionally large takes. Inject within a safe workability time from site tests, typically not over one hour. High-speed high-shear mixers give better, more consistent grout: one 43 kg bag must be wetted with less than 20 liters of water. Batch water by calibrated tank or flow meter, cement and sand by weight.
sections.body: (p. 4-19) During mixing a measured volume of water is usually added first, then cement, then aggregate or filler (if applicable). Grout should generally be mixed for at least two minutes and then kept in continuous slow agitation in a holding tank before pumping. Ready-mix grout should be considered only where exceptionally large grout takes are anticipated. Grout should be injected within a maximum 'safe workability' time after mixing, determined from on-site tests but typically not over one hour. High-speed high-shear mixers produce higher quality, more consistent grout more quickly than paddle mixers: the large cement particle surface area of a single 43 kg bag must be wetted with less than 20 liters of water, so intimate blending is essential for efficient hydration. Water is typically batched by calibrated tank or flow meter; cement by weight, bagged or bulk from a silo; sand or fillers by weight from premeasured bags or a checked and weighed gage box; bulk materials need a method of controlling quantities by volume or weight. Admixtures usually come ready-proportioned to one bag of cement, or the operator adjusts the dosage.
key_points: Batch water first, then cement, then aggregate or filler
Mix at least two minutes, then keep in slow agitation in a holding tank
Ready-mix grout only where exceptionally large takes are expected
Inject within the safe workability time from site tests, typically not over one hour
High-shear mixing needed: a 43 kg bag is wetted with less than 20 liters of water
Water by calibrated tank or flow meter; cement and sand by weight

sections.title: Gravity Fill Techniques (Type A Micropiles)
sections.summary: Type A: drill to depth, fill with grout by tremie from the bottom until grout like that injected flows from the mouth, place the reinforcement; no excess pressure (primary treatment). Neat cement, w/c 0.45 to 0.50 by weight; European sanded mixes up to 1:1 or 2:1 sand:cement, w/c often extended to 0.60 if stable (bleed under 5 percent). Gravity fill is now used mainly in rock or for low-capacity piles in stiff to hard cohesive soils; U.S. sanded mixes only for pregrouting, e.g., karst.
sections.body: (pp. 4-19 to 4-20) For Type A micropiles the hole is drilled to depth, filled with grout and the reinforcement placed. Grout should always be introduced through a tremie pipe exiting at the bottom of the hole and pumped until grout of similar quality to that injected flows freely from the mouth of the borehole, with no excess pressure; this phase is the primary treatment. The grout is usually a neat cement mix with w/c between 0.45 and 0.50 by weight. Sanded mixes of up to 1:1 or 2:1 sand:cement have been used in European practice but are becoming less common with the trend to higher grouting pressures with neat cement grouts. Gravity fill is now used mainly when the pile is founded in rock, or for low-capacity piles in stiff or hard cohesive soils where pressure grouting is unnecessary (Bruce and Gemme, 1992). For sanded mixes the w/c ratio is often extended to 0.60 if the mix stays stable (bleed less than 5 percent, no sand segregation) (Barley and Woodward, 1992). In the U.S., sanded mixes are only used for pregrouting, e.g., in karst, for economic reasons.
key_points: Tremie from the bottom until grout of injected quality flows from the mouth; no excess pressure (primary treatment)
Neat cement grout, w/c 0.45 to 0.50 by weight
European sanded mixes up to 1:1 or 2:1 sand:cement; w/c often extended to 0.60 if bleed under 5 % (Barley and Woodward, 1992)
Gravity fill now used mainly in rock or for low-capacity piles in stiff to hard cohesive soils (Bruce and Gemme, 1992)
In the U.S., sanded mixes only for pregrouting (e.g., karst)
sections.applicability: Tremie grouting of Type A micropiles and sanded mixes.

sections.title: Pressure Grouting Through the Casing (Type B Micropiles)
sections.summary: Type B: added grout is injected under pressure after tremie grouting as the temporary casing is withdrawn, over the bond length or full length, via a pressure cap; measure pressure near the injection point (gauge on the rig or at the cap). U.S. practice: average 0.5 to 1 MPa (72 to 145 psi); maximum typically 20 kPa/m (18 psi/ft) of depth in loose soils, 40 kPa/m (36 psi/ft) in dense soils, limited by heave, drilling system, casing seal, casing seizing, bond needed and depth. Pressure filtration and redensification raise skin friction.
sections.body: (pp. 4-20 to 4-21) For Type B micropiles additional grout is injected under pressure after the primary grout has been tremied and as the temporary casing is withdrawn, to enhance grout-to-ground bond; this may be limited to the load transfer length in the bearing stratum or extended to the full pile length. A pressure cap is attached to the top of the drill casing (often the drill head itself) and grout injected under controlled pressure; the old method of pressurizing with compressed air through the grout line is obsolete with modern pumps and stable neat grouts. Pressures are measured as close to the point of injection as possible: usually a gauge on the rig guides the driller's rate of casing withdrawal, or a gauge on the cap where casing is pulled by jacks; practitioners typically record the gauge pressure without correcting for line losses, reasoning they are offset by the grout column weight; the recommended method is a gauge on the drill rig or on the line just at the cap. American practice injects at a typical average pressure of 0.5 to 1 MPa (72 to 145 psi) to reinstate lateral soil pressures reduced by drilling and to permeate coarse granular soils or fractured rocks. Maximum pressures (typically 20 kPa per meter (18 psi per ft) of depth in loose soils and 40 kPa per meter (36 psi per ft) in dense soils) are dictated by: avoiding ground heave or uncontrolled grout loss; the drilling system (lower for augers, which leak at joints and around flights); the ground's ability to seal around the casing; avoiding seizing the casing by flash setting; the required bond capacity; and total depth. Pressure grouting improves skin friction, as ground anchor experience confirms. In granular soils some permeation and displacement (slight redensification repairing soil loosened by drilling) occurs, and pressure filtration forces mixing water out of the grout, leaving lower-water, quicker-setting, stronger grout and a cement cake at the interface that improves bond; in cohesive soils some displacement, compaction or local improvement occurs, generally less than in cohesionless soils. Pressure grouting also appears to recompact the soil and increase the effective bond-zone diameter, and may improve the soil between piles.
key_points: Type B: grout injected under pressure after tremie grouting, during casing withdrawal, over the bond length or full length
Pressure cap on the casing; measure pressure near the injection point (gauge on the rig or at the cap)
U.S. practice: average injection pressure 0.5 to 1 MPa (72 to 145 psi)
Maximum pressure typically 20 kPa/m (18 psi/ft) of depth in loose soils, 40 kPa/m (36 psi/ft) in dense soils
Limits: heave or grout loss, drilling system (augers lower), casing seal, casing seizing, required bond, depth
Pressure filtration and redensification increase skin friction and effective bond-zone diameter; less effect in cohesive soils
sections.applicability: Type B pressure grouting: method, pressures, limiting factors and mechanisms.

sections.title: Postgrouting (Type C and D Micropiles)
sections.summary: Where casing pressure cannot be held or no casing is used, grout is post-injected through sleeved tubes after primary grouting (Figure 4-13); neat grout, w/c 0.50 to 0.75. Type C: 15 to 25 minutes after primary grouting, one injection from the head without a packer through a 38- to 50-mm (1.5- to 2-in.) sleeved pipe at 1 MPa (145 psi) or more. Type D: after the primary grout hardens, several phases at 2 to 8 MPa (290 to 1,160 psi), usually 24 hours or more apart; up to 250 percent of the primary volume. Tube a manchette or circulating loop (Figures 4-14, 4-15).
sections.body: (pp. 4-21 to 4-26) High grout pressures may not be possible during casing removal because of hydrofracture or leakage around the casing, and some methods use no temporary casing, so Type B grouting is not feasible; post-grouting injects additional grout through special grout tubes some time after primary grouting (Figure 4-13). These grouts are always neat cement-water mixes (for pumpability through the rubber valves), possibly with higher w/c than the primary grout, 0.50 to 0.75 by weight; excess water is reasoned to be expelled by pressure filtration, so the placed grout is stronger. High postgrouting pressures are applied locally for restricted periods (a few minutes per sleeve); higher bond may in fact be achieved more efficiently in Type B micropiles, with lower pressures over a larger area and longer time. Type C: neat cement grout placed as for Type A; between 15 and 25 minutes later, before the primary grout hardens, similar grout is injected once from the head of the hole without a packer through a 38- to 50-mm (1.5- to 2-in.) preplaced sleeved grout pipe through the reinforcement at a pressure of at least 1 MPa (145 psi) (Figure 4-14). Type D: neat cement grout placed as for Type A; when it has hardened, similar grout is injected through a preplaced sleeved pipe, in several possible phases at selected horizons, typically recording 2 to 8 MPa (290 to 1,160 psi), especially at the start of each sleeve treatment when the primary grout is first ruptured; usually at least 24 hours between phases; three or four phases are not uncommon, adding as much as 250 percent of the primary volume. The postgrout tube can be a separate 25- or 38-mm (1- or 1.5-in.) sleeved plastic pipe (tube a manchette) placed with the reinforcement (Figure 4-13) or the sleeved reinforcement tube itself (Figure 4-14), grouted from the bottom sleeve upward with a double packer. Alternatively, a circulating loop from the surface raises pressure by closing the outlet valve until grout breaks out through one or more sleeves at the critical pressure; successive phases are assumed to open different sleeves, which only the tube a manchette with double packers guarantees (Figure 4-15). Where structural capacity depends on grout strength, avoid low-strength bentonite primary grouts used to reduce break-out pressures.
key_points: Postgrouting where casing pressure cannot be held or no casing is used: grout through sleeved tubes after primary grout (Figure 4-13)
Postgrout always neat cement, w/c 0.50 to 0.75 by weight; pressure filtration lowers placed water content
Type C: one injection 15 to 25 min after primary grout, from the head without packer, 38-50 mm sleeved pipe, at least 1 MPa (145 psi)
Type D: after primary grout hardens, several phases at 2 to 8 MPa (290 to 1,160 psi), usually 24 h apart; up to 250 % of primary volume
Type B may achieve bond more efficiently (lower pressure over larger area and longer time)
Tube a manchette (25 or 38 mm sleeved pipe) or sleeved reinforcement tube, double packer from the bottom up (Figure 4-14)
Circulating loop: different sleeves assumed to open each phase; only tube a manchette with double packers guarantees it (Figure 4-15)
Avoid low-strength bentonite primary grouts where structural capacity relies on grout strength
figures: Figure 4-13: Principle of the Tube a Manchette Method of Postgrouting Injection (p. 4-23)
Figure 4-14: Use of Reinforcement Tube as a Tube a Manchette Postgrouting System (p. 4-24)
Figure 4-15: Circulating Loop Arrangement for Pressure Grouting (DSI, 1992) (p. 4-25)
sections.applicability: Postgrouting through sleeved pipes for Type C and D micropiles.

sections.title: Top-Off (Secondary) Grouting
sections.summary: Grout levels commonly drop slightly before stiffening (seepage, bleed, shrinkage). Unlike ground anchors, where the hole is topped off later, a micropile without a permanent upper casing should not have a cold joint, since the grout column must be continuous for load and corrosion protection; top off during the stiffening phase. High-strength non-shrink grout may be considered where high bond to an existing structure is needed.
sections.body: (p. 4-26) Because of slow grout seepage, bleed or shrinkage the grout level commonly drops slightly before stiffening and hardening. In ground anchorage practice this is rectified by topping off later with the lowest water-content grout practical, but in micropile practice without a permanent casing reinforcing the upper length such a cold joint should be avoided, since the grout column should be continuous for load holding and corrosion protection; topping off is best done during the stiffening phase. Where particularly high interfacial bond stresses must be resisted between the micropile and an existing structure, a high-strength non-shrink grout may be considered.
key_points: Grout level commonly drops slightly before stiffening (seepage, bleed, shrinkage)
Without a permanent upper casing, avoid a cold joint: the grout column must be continuous for load and corrosion protection
Top off during the stiffening phase
Consider high-strength non-shrink grout for high bond to an existing structure
sections.applicability: Topping off the grout column without a cold joint.

sections.title: Reinforcing Steel
sections.summary: Reinforcing steel is treated under 4.4.1 General, 4.4.2 Placement of Reinforcement and 4.4.3 Reinforcement Types; no text is printed under this heading.
sections.body: (p. 4-26) No text is printed under this heading; see 4.4.1 General, 4.4.2 Placement of Reinforcement and 4.4.3 Reinforcement Types.
key_points: Reinforcing steel: general (4.4.1), placement (4.4.2), types and properties (4.4.3, Tables 4-2 to 4-5)
sections.applicability: Pointer to the reinforcing steel subsections (4.4.1 to 4.4.3).

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Reinforcement is set by the load supported and the stiffness needed to limit elastic displacement; it may be a single bar, a bar group, a steel pipe casing or rolled structural steel. American practice commonly uses a single bar and/or a high-strength steel casing.
sections.body: (p. 4-26) The amount of steel reinforcement in a micropile is determined by the loading it supports and the stiffness required to limit elastic displacements. Reinforcement may be a single reinforcing bar, a group of bars, a steel pipe casing or rolled structural steel. In American practice a single reinforcing bar and/or a high-strength steel casing is commonly used.
key_points: Amount set by load supported and stiffness needed to limit elastic displacement
Single bar, bar group, steel pipe casing or rolled structural steel
American practice: single bar and/or high-strength steel casing
sections.applicability: What sets the amount and form of micropile reinforcement.

sections.title: Placement of Reinforcement
sections.summary: Reinforcement is placed before grouting or into the grout-filled hole before temporary support is withdrawn; it must be clean of soil and mud, centralizers must be firmly fixed to keep the specified cover, and cages or groups must withstand installation, grouting and casing rotation and withdrawal.
sections.body: (p. 4-26) Reinforcement may be placed either before grouting or into the grout-filled borehole before the temporary support (if used) is withdrawn. It must be clean of deleterious substances such as surface soil and mud that may contaminate the grout or coat the reinforcement and impair bond. Suitable centralizers should be firmly fixed to maintain the specified grout cover. Pile cages and reinforcement groups, if used, must be robust enough to withstand installation, grouting and the rotation and withdrawal of the temporary casing.
key_points: Placed before grouting or into the grout-filled hole before temporary support is withdrawn
Must be clean of soil and mud that impair bond
Centralizers firmly fixed to maintain the specified grout cover
Cages and groups must withstand installation, grouting and casing rotation and withdrawal
sections.applicability: Placing reinforcement cleanly and centred.

sections.title: Reinforcement Types
sections.summary: Rebar: ASTM A615/AASHTO M31 and A706, 420 and 520 MPa (60, 75 ksi), 25 to 63 mm (Table 4-2). Continuous-thread bars: DSI Threadbar (Figure 4-17, Table 4-3), Williams All-Thread; can be cut and coupled anywhere. Hollow-core bars drill the hole (Table 4-4); main drawback cost. Pipe: ASTM A53, A519, A252, A106 at 241 MPa (36 ksi), or API 5CT/5L N-80 at 552 MPa (80 ksi), used by most higher capacity U.S. micropiles (Table 4-5); threaded joints reduce area. Composite bar and partial casing (Figure 4-18).
sections.body: (pp. 4-26 to 4-34) Concrete reinforcing steel bars (rebar): standard bars (Table 4-2) conforming to ASTM A615/AASHTO M31 and ASTM A706, yield strengths 420 and 520 MPa (60 and 75 ksi), diameters 25 to 63 mm (1 to 2.5 in.); a single bar is typical but bar groups are used, separated by spacers or tied to helical reinforcement so grout flows between the bars (Figure 4-16), or bundled with adequate development length; mechanical couplers are used where full-length bars cannot be placed in low overhead. Continuous-thread steel bars, such as the DSI Threadbar (GEWI) (Figure 4-17, Table 4-3), a common choice worldwide, with a coarse rolled thread, 19 to 63 mm (3/4 to 2-1/2 in.) in ASTM A615/AASHTO M31 steel at 420, 520 and 550 MPa (60, 75 and 80 ksi), 32 to 63 mm most common; higher strength ASTM A722/AASHTO M275 bars (ultimate 1,035 MPa (150 ksi)) in 26, 32 and 36 mm; the Williams All-Thread Bar, 20 to 89 mm (0.8 to 3.5 in.) in A615/M31 and 26 to 65 mm (1 to 2.5 in.) in A722/M275 (1,035 MPa (150 ksi) ultimate), with a finer thread. The thread gives grout-to-steel bond, allows cutting anywhere and coupling to restore full capacity, and simplifies connections with a hex nut and plate. Continuous-thread hollow-core bars (Dywidag, Ischebeck Titan, MAI International, Chance IBO) (Table 4-4) are drilled in with a bit on the tip and grout or air/water flush through the core; the main drawback is higher cost. Steel pipe casing gives large steel area, stiffness, high shear and reasonable bending for lateral loads; the drill casing is left as full-length reinforcement typically only for piles founded in rock, or a smaller permanent pipe is placed inside it; section length is set by mast and overhead clearance; sections are joined by machined threads whose reduced area should be considered in design, particularly for tension and bending, though joints can be reinforced to full strength. Pipe in ASTM A53, A519, A252 and A106 typically yields at 241 MPa (36 ksi), with low yield and very high unit cost. API 5CT or 5L (N-80) casing, 552 MPa (80 ksi), aids high loads and threaded joint strength, is available as mill secondary material at reasonable cost, and has been used for the overwhelming majority of higher capacity U.S. micropiles; specify ASTM A252 Grade 3 tensile requirements with minimum elongation of 15 percent but the design yield strength, and require at least two coupon samples or mill certificates per truckload. N-80 needs special welding procedures per AWS D1.1 (or an approved AWS weld procedure), submitted for owner approval; not needed for minor non-structural welds (Table 4-5). Composite reinforcement: with partial-length permanent casing (Types 1C, 2C, 4C), a bar reinforces the bottom portion and may extend to the top for tension (Figure 4-18); the reinforcement transition needs particular attention.
key_points: Rebar: ASTM A615/AASHTO M31 and A706, yield 420 and 520 MPa (60, 75 ksi), 25 to 63 mm (Table 4-2); bar groups with spacers (Figure 4-16)
DSI Threadbar (GEWI): 19 to 63 mm at 420, 520, 550 MPa, 32 to 63 mm most common; A722 bars 1,035 MPa ultimate in 26, 32, 36 mm (Table 4-3)
Williams All-Thread: 20 to 89 mm (A615) and 26 to 65 mm (A722, 1,035 MPa ultimate); finer thread
Continuous thread allows cutting anywhere, coupling to full capacity and hex-nut plate connections
Hollow-core bars (Dywidag, Titan, MAI, IBO) drill the hole with grout or air/water flush (Table 4-4); main drawback cost
Pipe: drill casing left full length typically only for piles in rock; threaded joints reduce area for tension and bending
ASTM A53, A519, A252, A106 pipe typically 241 MPa (36 ksi); API N-80 casing 552 MPa (80 ksi), used by most higher capacity U.S. micropiles (Table 4-5)
N-80: specify A252 Grade 3 tensile requirements, 15 % minimum elongation; two coupons or mill certificates per truckload; special welding per AWS D1.1
Composite: bar below partial-length casing (Types 1C, 2C, 4C), transition needs attention (Figure 4-18)
